title: Prudence (ST II-II.47)
hook: right reason in action, the charioteer of the virtues

segments.voice: Yesterday, habitus: a settled readiness to act, built by repeated acts, a virtue when it's good. Your line was we become our habits. Did you take the first step of your tiny habit? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

"Be ye therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves." Jesus says it to his disciples as he sends them out, in the Douay-Rheims, and it's a strange pairing. Serpents and doves. Shrewd and innocent at the same time. On a given day, managing one or the other can feel like plenty. Yesterday Thomas said virtues are good habits. Now he starts naming them, and he begins with the one he thinks steers the rest. It isn't the flashy one. It's the one that asks, before you move: what, here, actually needs doing? Today's word: prudence.
screen: `WISE AS SERPENTS, SIMPLE AS DOVES.` → `VIRTUES ARE GOOD HABITS.` → `THE ONE THAT STEERS THE REST.`

segments.voice: In everyday English, prudence can sound like carefulness, saving money, never taking a risk. Thomas means something bigger. Following Aristotle, he calls prudence right reason applied to action. It's practical wisdom: seeing, in this situation, with these people, what the good thing to do actually is. Generous people, brave people, fair people, all still need to know how to be generous or brave or fair today. The Catechism calls prudence the charioteer of the virtues. The other virtues are the horses. Prudence holds the reins. Thomas breaks prudence into three steps. First, take counsel: look at the options, ask, remember what's worked before. Second, judge: decide which option is right. Third, command: actually do it. And here's the surprise. Thomas says the chief act of prudence is the third one, the command. Not the thinking. The doing. A person who weighs everything beautifully and never acts isn't prudent. They've stopped halfway. He also warns about fakes. Cleverness at getting a bad goal is craftiness, not prudence. And on this account, caution that never moves is not the virtue either. So the serpent and the dove fit together after all. The serpent's part is clear sight about how things really are. The dove's part is a clean aim. Prudence is both, ending in an act. This week walked from evil as a lack, through soul and body, mind and will, Thomas's test of happiness, seeing God and habits, to prudence. Tomorrow, the next virtue.
screen: `NOT JUST CAREFULNESS.` · `RIGHT REASON APPLIED TO ACTION.` · `COUNSEL, JUDGE, COMMAND.` · `THE CHIEF ACT IS THE DOING.` · then, large: `WISE AS SERPENTS, SIMPLE AS DOVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one prudent pause. Settle, and breathe. Bring up one decision waiting on you, something you'll have to act on soon. Walk Thomas's three steps slowly. First, counsel. What are the real options? Who could you ask? What happened last time? Second, judgment. Of these, which is right, here, now, with these people? Let one rise to the top. Third, command. What is the very first concrete act, and when will you do it? Name the hour. If you pray, you can ask for light on the choice. The bell holds the time.
Prudence. Right reason applied to action: taking counsel, judging, and then doing, which Thomas calls its chief act. Today's word.
Your line: think, then act. Today, before one decision, take a breath for counsel, choose, and then follow through. That's the week. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching names prudence first among the four cardinal virtues, and Catholics often speak of discernment, seeking counsel and praying before a big decision, as the practice of it.

what a scholar hears: Thomas, after Aristotle, calls it right reason applied to action, with counsel, judgment and command, command chief.

notes: All Aquinas is paraphrased. Check: prudence as right reason applied to action, following Aristotle (II-II.47.2); counsel, judgment and command, with command as the chief act (II-II.47.8); craftiness (astutia) as a false prudence (II-II.55.3).
'The charioteer of the virtues' (auriga virtutum) is attributed to the Catechism (CCC 1806), paraphrased, not quoted.
'Caution that never moves is not the virtue either' is the script's gloss on command being the chief act; check it doesn't overstate Thomas.
'Managing one or the other can feel like plenty' is a light aside, not a factual claim; cut if the editor prefers.
Week boundary: this day closes the week of days 1163–1169.
